relief requested:
In the Statement of Claim, Claimant requested: 
1. Expungement of the Underlying Claim from his CRD record pursuant to FINRA 
Rule 2080(b)(1)(A) as the claim, allegation, or information is factually impossible 
or clearly erroneous; 
2. Expungement of the Underlying Claim from his CRD record pursuant to FINRA 
Rule 2080(b)(1)(C) as the claim, allegation, or information is false; 
3. An award of compensatory damages in the amount of $1.00 from the 
Respondent; and 
4. Any and all other relief that the Arbitrator deems just and equitable. 

In the Statement of Answer, Respondent did not set forth a specific relief request. 
AWARD: The undersigned Arbitrator has decided and determined in full and final 
resolution of the issues submitted for determination as follows: 

1. The Arbitrator recommends the expungement of all references to occurrence 
number 1426079, from registration records maintained by the CRD, for Claimant 
Robert Howard Keller (CRD# 2168444), with the understanding that, pursuant to 
Notice to Members 04-16, Claimant Robert Howard Keller must obtain confirmation 

from a court of competent jurisdiction before the CRD will execute the expungement 
directive. 

Unless specifically waived in writing by FINRA, parties seeking judicial confirmation 
of an arbitration award containing expungement relief must name FINRA as an 
additional party and serve FINRA with all appropriate documents. 

Pursuant to Rule 13805 of the Code of Arbitration Procedure, the Arbitrator has 
made the following Rule 2080 affirmative findings of fact: 

The claim, allegation, or information is factually impossible or clearly erroneous; and 

The claim, allegation, or information is false. 

The Arbitrator has made the above Rule 2080 findings based on the following 
reasons: 

The customer that filed the Underlying Claim (“Customer”) and Claimant had an 
excellent business relationship that began years before said allegation, and 
continued following said allegations. 

In the summer of 2008, Claimant made a recommendation that the Customer 
purchase an investment grade preferred stock of a large bank. The stock was 
recommended by the Respondent’s syndicate department as suitable for the 
Customer’s investor profile and it was familiar to the Customer as she had 
purchased similar investments in the past. 

The Customer agreed with the recommendation and elected to purchase 2,000 
shares of the stock at a price of $25.00 per share, which amounted to less than 10% 
of her portfolio. The Customer’s purchase was underwritten by Respondent. 

In the fall of 2008, the stock market declined dramatically, as a result of an 
unprecedented financial crisis. As a result of said crisis, preferred stocks of banks 
began to weaken, as did the Customer’s stock. 

Claimant discussed the financial crisis and the resulting state of her stock with the 
Customer. Per the Customer’s authorization, Claimant liquidated 2,000 shares of the 
bank stock. 

Shortly after, the Customer stated to the Claimant that she only intended to sell 
1,000 shares rather than 2,000 shares. 

To remedy the situation, Claimant processed a trade correction to put 1,000 shares 
back into the Customer’s account. Said correction incurred a $300.00 loss which 
was then charged against Claimant, per Respondent’s policy at the time. 

The Customer’s situation was fully remedied by the aforementioned action of 
Claimant. However, because the Customer made the request to reinstate her 1,000 
shares in writing, it was logged as a complaint and appeared on Claimant’s CRD. 

As of September 16, 2009, Respondent denied the Customer’s claims that Claimant 
made an unauthorized trade and unsuitable investment recommendations. 
OTHER ISSUES: The Arbitrator acknowledges that she has read the pleadings and 
other materials filed by the parties. 

Respondent did not oppose Claimant’s request for expungement. 

On March 23, 2017, Claimant filed a copy of a letter with FINRA Office of Dispute 
Resolution evidencing that the Customer was served with copies of the Case Information 
Sheet, Statement of Claim, and Initial Pre-Hearing Conference Scheduling Order setting 
the date for the expungement hearing. 

The Arbitrator conducted a recorded telephonic hearing on May 26, 2017 so the parties 
could present oral argument and evidence on Claimant’s request for expungement. The 
Customer did not appear at the expungement hearing. Claimant checked the tracking 
number for the package containing copies of the Case Information Sheet, Statement of 
Claim, and Initial Pre-Hearing Conference Scheduling Order setting the date for the 
expungement hearing, and the Customer did receive the notice of the hearing, and the 
claim and response and chose not to appear. 

During the expungement hearing, Claimant withdrew the request for $1.00 in damages. 

The Arbitrator notes that no settlement was reached as the Underlying Claim was denied 
by Respondent, and the Customer did not pursue the complaint further in either arbitration 
or litigation. As such, the Arbitrator determined there were no settlement documents to 
review. 

The Arbitrator notes that Claimant did not previously file a claim requesting 
expungement of same disclosure. 

In recommending expungement, the Arbitrator relied upon the following documentary or 
other evidence: Statement of Claim including attached exhibits 1-4; Statement of 
Answer; telephonic testimony of Claimant; and Claimant’s BrokerCheck® Report.

and for Palm Beach County, Florida, issued a preliminary injunction enjoining Claimants 
from pursuing their claims in arbitration against Respondents GFIS, Costa and 
Conness. Accordingly, the Panel made no determinations with respect to any of the 
claims asserted against these Respondents in the Statement of Claim. 
On or about June 27, 2018, Respondent Madison filed a Motion to Dismiss, asserting 
that dismissal is warranted pursuant to Rule 12504(a)(6)(B) of the Code because 
Respondent Madison was not associated with the accounts, securities or conduct at 
issue in this matter. Specifically, Respondent Madison stated, among other things, that 
Claimants were never its clients, Respondent Madison never transacted any business 
with them, and there is no executed arbitration agreement between them. In their 
opposition thereto, Claimants asserted they transacted business with Global Wealth 
Management ("GWM"), bought and maintained investments with GWM, received advice 
and guidance on their Woodbridge securities investment from GWM, and believed that 
the personnel at GWM were managing them. Claimants allege that since GWM is the 
alter ego of Respondents Costa and Conness, who are registered representatives of 
Respondent Madison, Claimants were customers of Madison. In its Reply, Respondent 
Madison stated that it and GWM are not now, and never have been affiliated entities, 
and that GWM is an independent financial services firm, which was founded by its 
managing directors, Respondents Costa and Conness, while they were still affiliated 
with Respondent GFIS. 
On October 22, 2018, the Panel heard oral arguments on Respondent Madison's 
Motion to Dismiss during a recorded telephonic conference with the parties. On or 
about October 26, 2018, the Panel granted Respondent Madison's Motion to Dismiss 
pursuant to Rule 12504 of the Code. Specifically, the Panel found as follows: 
"The Panel is cognizant of FIN RA's policy that, prior to the conclusion of a 
party's case in chief, a Motion to Dismiss is discouraged. However, after 
car -consideration of the Statement of Claim and the arguments 
presented at the prehearing conference call and in the review of all 
documents, the Panel found no basis for imposing liability on Respondent 
Madison for losses sustained by Claimants. The moving party had no 
connection to the purchase of the subject securities, or to any fraud or 
misrepresentation related thereto. There is no basis for imposition of 
liability for failure to supervise, as there was no duty of Respondent 
Madison to supervise anyone connected with the subject securities. There 
is no contract between Respondent Madison and Claimants. While the 
Panel are loathe to deny Claimants an opportunity to present their case on 
the merits, in this instance there is no evidence which could support an 
award against Respondent Madison."

may be executed in counterpart copies or that a handwritten, signed Award may be 
entered.

The Arbitrator has made the above Rule 2080 findings based on the following 
reasons: 

When the Customers became clients of Claimant in February 1999, they stated 
an interest in growth with an aggressive risk tolerance, low liquidity needs and a 
ten year timeline. Claimant recommended a balanced portfolio and included an 
option to supplement the core investments. Mr. M requested more technology 
stocks and none of the bonds, which occurred. From that day forward, the parties

cordial relationship. Before Claimant made any trade, he conferred with the

from registration records maintained by th e CRD with the understanding that, 
pursuant to Notice to Members 04 -16, Claimants Pamela R. Raben, Brent Taylor 
Henry, and Dustin Clay Colebank must obtain confirmation from a court of 
competent jurisdiction before the CRD will execute the expungement directive. 

Unless specifically waived in writing by FINRA, parties seeking judicial 
confirmation of an arbitration award containing expungement relief must name 
FINRA as an additional party and serve FINRA with all appropriate documents. 

Pursuant to Rule 13805 of the Code of Arbitration Procedure (“Code”), the 
Arbitrator has made the following Rule 2080 affirmative findings of fact: 

The claim, allegation, or information is factually impossible or clearly 
erroneous. 

The registered person was not involved in the alleged investment-related 
sales practice violation, forgery, theft, misappropriation, or conversion of 
funds. 

The claim, allegation, or information is false. 

The Arbitrator has made the above Rule 2080 findings based on the following 
reasons: 

Occurrence Numbers 1625525 and 1622140–Henry and Colebank 

Mr. B was Henry’s long-time friend. He opened a brokerage account with 
Respondent and became Henry and Colebank’s client. At some point during 
the business relationship, Mr. B asked for assistance in purchasing a life 
insurance policy, intended for use as a vehicle to permit the university where 
he had coached for decades, to pay off debt. Shortly after, Henry and 
Colebank referred Mr. B to an insurance representative in Respondent’s 
insurance department. 

Henry and Colebank both testified that to their knowledge, the insurance 
representative explained all details of the policy to Mr. B and provided him 
with all pertinent written materials, and Mr. B acknowledged in writing that he 
understood the details and authorized the investment. Neither Henry nor 
Colebank recommended, were primarily responsible for making, or made any 
detailed disclosures about the policy. Although Henry was present for further 
discussions about the policy, he did not take a lead role and both Henry and 
Colebank’s involvement, appeared to be limited to the referral. 

In or around December 2009, Mr. L was named trustee of Mr. B’s life 
insurance trust and between 2008 and 2012, Henry and Colebank spoke to 
Mr. B regarding the performance of his investment portfolio. Neither Mr. B nor 
Mr. L ever expressed any dissatisfaction with the policy and as far as they 
knew, based on their limited involvement, the policy was fully and accurately 
discussed in great detail with Mr. B and ultimately sold as Mr. B wished. In 
fact, this dispute appears to have arisen because Mr. B’s heirs wanted 
Respondent to assist them in liquidating the policy and Respondent refused 
because doing so was against company policy. In any event, the policy was 
sold. 

However, neither Henry nor Colebank told Mr. B that he could sell the policy 
or made any representations to that effect, and neither had any knowledge 
that anyone involved in the sale of the policy told Mr. B that was an option. 

Occurrence Numbers 1967257 and 1967290–Henry and Raben 

Ms. K’s allegations relate to a mortgage obtained by Ms. K and her former 
husband, which they recognized as valid and paid for at least a decade 
before Ms. K claimed that her signature had been “forged.” In fact, Ms. K 
repeatedly claimed a mortgage interest deduction for the mortgage on her 
federal income tax returns and also acknowledged the existence and validity 
of the mortgage on numerous occasions, including under oath before the U.S. 
Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arkansas and in court filings concerning 
her divorce. Ms. K’s assertions that her signature had been forged during 
creation of the mortgage and that she did not know of its existence are clearly 
erroneous, factually impossible, and false. 

In addition, Henry and Raben are not in the business of recommending or 
approving mortgages and did not do so in this matter; they merely referred 
Ms. K and her then-husband to the appropriate department to seek a 
mortgage. They were not involved with the evaluation of the mortgage 
application or approval process, and made no representations concerning the 
mortgage. Moreover, Raben testified that she did not notarize a “forged” 
signature and neither she nor Henry were aware of a “forged” signature. 

Additionally, there is no credible evidence that Ms. K’s signature was forged. 
Indeed, that claim was rejected by an Arkansas state appellate court, as 
admitted by Ms. K in her submission to FINRA ODR. It appears that Ms. K 
also raised that allegation in the bankruptcy court, to no avail. Finally, neither 
Henry nor Raben were in a position to make any “misappropriation” as to the 
mortgage. The evidence clearly demonstrated that they were not involved in 
any alleged investment-related sales practice violation, forgery, or 
misappropriation. 

2. Any and all claims for relief not specifically addressed herein are denied.

After considering the pleadings, the testimony and evidence presented at the expungement 
hearing, and any post-hearing submissions, the Panel has decided in full and final resolution of 
the issues submitted for determination as follows: 
1. The Panel recommends the expungement of all references to Occurrence Numbers 
1661725, 1488932, 650346, 179622, 361572, and 607364 from registration records 
maintained by the CRD for Claimant Virginia Frances Thompson (CRD 1834046) with the 
understanding that, pursuant to Notice to Members 04-16, Claimant Virginia Frances 
Thompson must obtain confirmation from a court of competent jurisdiction before the CRD 
will execute the expungement directive. 
Unless specifically waived in writing by FINRA, parties seeking judicial confirmation of an 
arbitration award containing expungement relief must name FINRA as an additional party 
and serve FINRA with all appropriate documents. 
Pursuant to Rule 13805 of the Code of Arbitration Procedure (“Code”), the Panel has made 
the following Rule 2080 affirmative findings of fact as to all Occurrences:
The claim, allegation, or information is factually impossible or clearly erroneous.
The claim, allegation, or information is false.
The Panel has made the above Rule 2080 findings based on the following reasons: 
Occurrence Number 1661725
The recommendations were suitable for these customers (husband and wife) at the time 
Claimant made them, given the customers’ moderately aggressive risk tolerance and the 
wife’s decision to double the amount of money she was withdrawing from the account, which 
necessitated reallocating the account so that it would generate more income so that she 
would not be drawing down as much of her principal balance. The allegation that Claimant 
made unsuitable and speculative recommendations is false. In addition, Claimant was not 
the financial advisor responsible for monitoring the investment when the customers moved 
the account elsewhere.
Occurrence Number 1488932 
The annuity was suitable for this customer and it was suitable to not include a “living benefit” 
rider given that the customer was very clear that, considering his net worth and annual 
expenses, the funds from that particular annuity would not be needed during his lifetime. As 
such, the variable annuity was a suitable recommendation at the time it was made and the 
allegation that Claimant “removed” the living benefit rider from the annuity application is 
false.
Occurrence Number 650346 
The investment was suitable for this customer at the time of the recommendation, with all 
risks explained. The customer, who was a moderately aggressive investor seeking income, 
purchased approximately four or five income-producing investments, including funds and 
bonds, with the approximately $100,000.00 she held with Claimant. Specifically, as it relates 
to Service Merchandise bonds, it would have been impossible to predict the events that 
ultimately led to the bond's decline. The BrokerCheck® Report indicates that Claimant 
contributed $2,000.00 to the settlement amount. That is inaccurate. The disclosure was 
reported by Claimant as the broker and, upon information and belief, she incorrectly marked 
that she contributed to the settlement amount when in fact she had not. The allegations 
contained in this occurrence are false and without merit.
Occurrence Number 179622
The recommendation to purchase the bonds was not inappropriate. This customer had a 
net worth of between $350,000.00 and $400,000.00. Her investment objective was income 
and she expressed that she was willing to take on additional risk by investing in high yield 
bonds that pay higher yields that she stated she needed, rather than the more conservative 
bonds offered. After the discussion, Claimant determined that investing in several high-yield 
bonds would be an appropriate recommendation because they would provide the higher 
yields she was seeking and by investing in several different bonds it would lower her overall 
risk through diversification. Claimant only recommended high-yield or non-investment grade 
bonds that were rated at least BB+ or BBB+. Claimant explained how high-yield bonds 
function and the difference between how they function compared to more conservative 
bonds, like government bonds. Once Claimant was satisfied that the customer understood, 
she recommended that the customer invest in several high-yield bonds. Understanding how 
high-yield bonds function and the reason for the recommendation, the customer decided to 
purchase approximately four to six of the high-yield bonds Claimant offered to her. The 
allegations contained in the claim are false.
Occurrence Number 361572 
The bonds were suitable for this customer at the time of the recommendation; therefore, the 
claim made in this matter is false. The customer was a moderately aggressive investor who 
was seeking to earn the maximum income from his investments with Claimant. Claimant 
presented the customer with numerous potential investments that would maximize his 
income. Out of the various investments Claimant presented to the customer, he was 
interested in the high-yield bonds she presented because of their yield. Claimant explained 
to the customer that high-yield bonds are considered to be lower quality and higher risk than 
certain other types of bonds. Over the approximately four years that the customer worked 
with Claimant, he decided to purchase approximately six high-yield bonds. In May 2007, 
Claimant left PaineWebber, now Respondent UBS, for another firm. The customer decided 
not to move his accounts to Claimant’s new firm and because he had a relationship with a 
senior broker prior to Claimant, his accounts were assigned to two other advisors at 
PaineWebber. Approximately two years after Claimant left PaineWebber and the customer 
ceased to be her client, three of the six bonds he purchased from Claimant declined in value 
and the customer complained that the bonds were not suitable investments. Notably, he did 
not complain that the other high-yield bonds that did not decline in value were unsuitable, nor 
did he consider the bonds to be unsuitable at any time prior. The BrokerCheck® Report 
indicates that Claimant contributed $16,000.00 to the settlement amount. That is inaccurate. 
The disclosure was reported by Claimant as the broker and, upon information and belief, she 
incorrectly marked that she contributed to the settlement amount when in fact she had not.
Occurrence Number 607364
The investment was suitable for the customers’ (husband and wife) portfolio at the time of 
the recommendation, with all risks explained. Claimant offered the customers several 
investment options that were in line with their stated moderately aggressive risk tolerance 
and investment objective of income. Several of the options Claimant presented to the 
customers were high-yield bonds—Claimant only recommended high-yield or non-
investment grade bonds that were rated at least BB+ or BBB+. Subsequently, the husband 
passed away and the son was appointed as successor co-trustee of the trust at issue (the 
“Trust”). It is important to note that the son worked in the investment underwriting business. 
At the time and when the complaint at issue was made, Claimant met with the wife to review 
the portfolio. During the meeting, Claimant reviewed the portfolio and discussed the risks 
associated with its then current allocation. The wife expressed satisfaction with the holdings 
and her desire to maintain the portfolio positions. Additionally, neither the wife nor the son 
requested any changes to the portfolio be made subsequent to the husband’s passing. The 
allegations contained in this occurrence are false and without merit

Respondent Epinger, as regional director, was responsible for hiring registered 
representatives, however, he was not responsible, nor did he hire the registered 
representative involved in this matter. Respondent Epinger was not responsible for the 
direct supervision of the registered representative or any registered representatives. A 
supervisory team was responsible for the direct supervision of the registered 
representatives. The supervisory team did not report to and was not supervised by

award:
After considering the pleadings, the testimony and evidence presented at the expungement 
hearing, the Arbitrator has decided in full and final resolution of the issues submitted for 
determination as follows: 
1. The Arbitrator awards the expungement of all references to Occurrence Numbers 1126430, 
1126429, 1444476, 1523952, 1587381, and 1563546 from registration records maintained 
by the CRD for Claimant John Edward Bostaph (CRD Number 2835105) with the 
understanding that, pursuant to Rule 2080, Claimant John Edward Bostaph must obtain 
confirmation from a court of competent jurisdiction before the CRD will execute the 
expungement directive. 
Unless specifically waived in writing by FINRA, parties seeking judicial confirmation of an 
arbitration award containing expungement relief must name FINRA as an additional party 
and serve FINRA with all appropriate documents. 
Pursuant to Rule 13805 of the Code, the Arbitrator has made the following affirmative 
findings of fact:
The registered person was not involved in the alleged investment-related sales practice 
violation, forgery, theft, misappropriation, or conversion of funds.
The claim, allegation, or information is false.
The Arbitrator has made the above findings based on the following reasons: 
Claimant seeks expungement of six different Occurrence Numbers from his CRD 
records. While each of these is different and will be discussed separately, they all have a 
few elements in common, which will be discussed as a whole.
All of these occurrences happened many years ago. Two of them happened in February 
2003 and four of them occurred between 2009 and 2011.
As such, documentation on these matters is minimal.
Three of the underlying clients in these matters are now deceased. Of those who are 
living, one could not be located and two were notified of this matter and did not respond.
In all of these matters, Claimant’s employers, whether WaMu or Wells Fargo, found no 
fault in Claimant’s actions and rejected the accuracy of the claims. While WaMu no 
longer exists, Wells Fargo does not oppose Claimant’s request for expungement. In 
addition, neither FINRA nor any other agency found any fault with Claimant’s actions.
In some of these cases, there was no settlement at all. In a few of the cases, Claimant’s 
employers settled for a minimal amount. Claimant did not contribute to any of the 
settlements. In only one case was there a settlement approaching the stated value of the 
claim, which was relatively small in any case.
In all of these cases, the complaints were made at a time when the financial markets had 
suffered significant reversals. In the first two matters, the complaints were made after 
Claimant had left the firm (WaMu) and was no longer in communication with the 
underlying client. In the later three cases, the complaints were made during a time where 
Claimant had suffered a severe injury and had undergone two surgeries and was no 
longer in contact with the underlying clients.
In general, Claimant explained extremely credibly and clearly his process for working with 
clients. He explained that he usually had a first meeting where he assessed the client in 
detail and discussed possible investment strategies, then a second meeting where he 
reviewed the recommended strategies in detail and then, usually, did not actually 
proceed with any investment until the third meeting so that the client had sufficient time to 
think about, understand and consider the investment strategy.
Claimant testified that he explained all of the details of each investment in great detail 
and satisfied himself that the client understood the investment completely including the 
level of risk involved. He also testified that all such investments had been reviewed by his 
employer, whether WaMu or Wells Fargo, and approved. Finally, he testified that he 
stayed in close touch with all clients to be sure they were happy with the investment and 
to answer any possible questions.
In nearly all of these cases, Claimant was no longer in communication with the client 
which he feels may account for why there was a complaint. He further believes that 
subsequent advisors, in an effort to get the client to initiate new transactions, had 
critiqued the previous investment strategy, which resulted in the complaints.
In the first two matters, Claimant was no longer in communication with the client because 
he had moved from WaMu to Wells Fargo and in the later three matters, he was no 
longer in communication with the client due to his injury and subsequent surgeries.
Occurrence Number 1126430
In this matter, Mr. C, was a customer of WaMu. He was also an employee of American 
Airlines. Claimant testified that Mr. C came into the bank one day in about late 2002 or 
early 2003 and wished to immediately purchase about $200,000 worth of American 
Airlines stock with some of the funds he had on deposit at WaMu. Claimant testified that 
he and others at WaMu explained to Mr. C that the commission rate for such a purchase 
would be quite high and they suggested that he transfer the funds to a discount broker 
and then buy the shares through the discount broker. Mr. C said that he had to buy the 
stock that day and couldn’t wait. Since Mr. C insisted on the purchase, Claimant felt 
obliged to follow his directions.
Apparently, the stock declined shortly thereafter by approximately $50,000. Mr. C filed a 
complaint with WaMu in early February 2003. Claimant testified that, in subsequent 
proceedings in the matter, it became clear that Mr. C’s wife had been unaware of the 
initial purchase and was extremely upset that it had occurred, that it had lost money and 
that the commission was relatively high. Claimant testified that it became clear that Mr. 
C’s wife had pressured him to file the complaint. The complaint was for $54,425 in 
damages, which was equal to the approximate amount of the decline in value of the stock 
($50,000), plus the commission on the transaction ($4,425). 
After an arbitration claim had been filed and in the course of the proceedings, WaMu 
eventually settled the matter for $2,200, essentially returning slightly under half of the 
commission fee.
Given that the purchase of the stock was entirely at Mr. C’s behest, not recommended by 
Claimant or anyone else at WaMu and that the commission fee was completely explained 
to Mr. C and he was, in fact, urged to purchase the stocks through a discount brokerage, 
I find that the claim by Mr. C was false. It is not of public value to have this false claim 
remain on Claimants CRD records and expungement is awarded.
Occurrence Number 1126429
In 1999, the underlying client, Mr. M, purchased a variable annuity. Claimant testified that 
Mr. M was a sophisticated investor who had experience with annuities and wished to 
transfer into a variable annuity for both tax reasons and because he believed they could 
provide greater return. Claimant testified that all aspects of the annuity, including the 
surrender schedule, were thoroughly explained to Mr. M and that he fully understood 
them. In addition, purchase of the annuity was approved by both WaMu compliance and 
the carrier of the annuity.
Four years later, in February of 2003, after Claimant had left WAMU, Mr. M filed a 
complaint alleging that he was not fully informed of the surrender schedule. He asked for 
damages of $15,328.39. Claimant believes that a new advisor had convinced Mr. M to 
get into another investment, the Mr. M was upset at the surrender fee on the annuity and 
had filed the complaint in order to recover all or part of the surrender fee. WaMu 
investigated the matter, found that it had no merit and denied the claim. There were no 
further proceedings.
Given Claimant’s very cogent, detailed and credible testimony on this matter, I find that 
the claim by Mr. M was false. It is not of public value to have this false claim remain on 
Claimant’s CRD records and expungement is awarded.
Occurrence Number 1444476
The underlying client in the matter, Ms. G, had been a customer of Wells Fargo for about 
four years when her account was transferred to Claimant. Therefore, he had not advised 
her when she had first set up the account, though he stated that he continued to monitor 
her account, after she became his client, in all aspects, including suitability.
Claimant testified that, at some point, Ms. G’s son became involved with the account. At 
one point, he called Wells Fargo’s call center and wanted to make some transactions in 
the account but was told he did not have the authority to do so. At another point, he 
attempted to get money out of the account, but was, again, told he did not have authority 
to do so. The son, did, eventually have a phone call with Claimant and his mother in 
which she authorized a transfer of funds to her son. Claimant testified that he believes 
Ms. G’s son was manipulating her in order to get funds from the account. Claimant 
testified that he believes that there is a good chance that the complaint that was filed 
under Ms. G’s name was actually written by her son and may have either been a forgery 
or signed by Ms. G under undue influence or duress. In any event, a complaint was filed 
on February 2, 2009, alleging failure to follow instructions and unsuitability. Damages of 
$5,000 were demanded. Wells Fargo investigated the complaint and denied it. No further 
action occurred.
Given Claimant’s extremely detailed and credible testimony in this matter, I find that: 
(a) Claimant was not involved in the initial transactions in Ms. G’s account and, therefore 
the allegation regarding suitability of the initial investment does not apply to Claimant; (b) 
Claimant monitored Ms. G’s account on an ongoing basis for all issues, including 
suitability, and, therefore, any allegation as to unsuitability during Claimant’s term as 
advisor is false; and (c) Claimant did not fail to follow proper instructions and, therefore, 
the allegations regarding that are false. It is not of public value to have this inaccurate 
and false claim remain on Claimant’s CRD records and expungement is awarded.
Occurrence Number 1523952
The underlying client in the matter, Ms. D, had been an existing client of Claimant for 
some time. Claimant testified that one investment of hers made initially in March 2008 
involving bonds had matured while Claimant was on leave due to his injury and 
subsequent surgeries and, apparently, she was unhappy with the performance. Claimant 
believes that this would not have occurred if he had been in communication with her, but 
that instead another broker, who was handling her account and trying to get her to invest 
further had criticized the previous investment. The Client filed a complaint on March 15, 
2010, stating that the investment had been unsuitable for her. She sought damages of 
$30,000.
Claimant testified very credibly that he had fully assessed her suitability for the 
investment, that it was entirely suitable, and that his manager had also reviewed the 
investment and found it fully suitable. Wells Fargo did not find any wrongdoing by 
Claimant, nor did FINRA or any other agency. While Claimant was on medical leave, 
Wells Fargo elected to settle the matter for approximately $27,000 rather than incur 
excessive legal fees.
Given Claimant’s very credible testimony on this matter, that the claim of “unsuitability” 
was made over two years after the initial investment and, especially, given the 
circumstances that he was on medical leave at the time the claim was filed and unable to 
be in communication with his client, I find that the claim by Ms. D was false. It is not of 
public value to have this false claim remain on Claimant’s CRD records and 
expungement is awarded. 
Occurrence Number 1587381
The underlying client in the matter, Mr. W, had been an existing customer of Wells Fargo 
bank for some time. Claimant testified that in about late 2006 or early 2007, Mr. W came 
into an inheritance. Claimant testified that he did a thorough and in-depth analysis of Mr. 
W’s needs, including his needs for retirement, and recommended two investments that 
he felt perfectly suited him, a First Trust unit investment trust and a Riversource Life 
variable annuity. Claimant testified that he explained the investments very carefully to Mr. 
W, that Mr. W entirely understood and approved of the investments and that Mr. W had a 
30 day right to cancel. Mr. W held the investments for approximately 4 or 5 years. 
However, on March 30, 2011, after Claimant had left Wells Fargo due to his medical 
issues, Mr. W. had filed a complaint alleging that the investments were unsuitable and 
seeking damages of a minimum of $70,000. Eight months later, Wells Fargo, without 
Claimant being involved, decided to settle for a fraction of the requested damages, 
$17,500, rather than incur further legal fees. There was no finding of wrongdoing by 
Claimant by Wells Fargo. 
Claimant, again, that he believes if he had been in communication with Mr. W no 
complaint would have been filed and that it is likely that after he left Wells Fargo a new 
broker, looking to generate business, criticized the previous investment. Given Claimant’s 
very cogent, detailed and credible testimony on this matter, I find that the claim by Mr. W 
was false. It is not of public value to have this false claim remain on Claimant’s CRD 
records and expungement is awarded. 
Occurrence Number 1563546
The underlying client in the matter, Ms. Z, was referred to Claimant by Wells Fargo bank 
and she had approximately $100,000 to invest. Claimant stated that he thoroughly 
reviewed her goals, met with her at least three times and determined that a market linked 
Certificate of Deposit was an appropriate, conservative investment for her with a buffer 
against loss. He testified that she was completely apprised of and understood the risk. 
The investment was approved by Wells Fargo and occurred on or about April 28, 2008. 
Unfortunately, due to the massive market crash in and about 2008-2009, the investment, 
apparently, declined slightly. A riskier investment would have declined ever further. On or 
about April 11, 2011, Ms. Z filed a complaint alleging that she had been guaranteed a 
100% return on the investment but instead it had declined, and she stated damages of 
$5,158.55. 
At this time, Claimant had left Wells Fargo due to his medical issues. Four months later, 
Wells Fargo settled for $5,158.55, a nominal sum considering the cost of potential 
litigation. Neither Wells Fargo nor anyone else found any wrongdoing on Claimant’s 
behalf. Given Claimant’s very detailed and extremely credible testimony on this matter, 
as well as the absurdity of Ms. Z’s claim that she was promised a 100% return within a 
two-year period on this investment, and the circumstances of the severe 2008-2009 
market crash, I find that the claim by Ms. Z was false. It is not of public value to have this 
false claim remain on Claimant’s CRD records and expungement is awarded.

case summary:
In the Statement of Claim, Claimants asserted the following causes of action: common law 
negligence, negligent misrepresentation and omission, unsuitability, breach of fiduciary duty, 
and breach of contract. The causes of action relate to investment in Healthcare Trust, Inc.
Unless specifically admitted in the Statement of Answer, Respondent denied the allegations made

other issues considered and decided:
The Arbitrator acknowledges having read the pleadings and other materials filed by the parties. 
On August 30, 2024, Respondent filed a Motion to Dismiss pursuant to Rule 12206 of the Code 
of Arbitration Procedure (“Code”). On October 18, 2024, Claimants filed a response opposing 
the Motion to Dismiss. On October 23, 2024, Respondent filed a reply in further support of the 
Motion to Dismiss. On October 29, 2024, the Arbitrator heard oral arguments on the Motion to 
Dismiss. On October 30, 2024, the Arbitrator granted the Motion to Dismiss on the grounds that:
Claimant filed a Claim for an Expedited Simplified Hearing “Special Proceeding” on May 3, 
2024, seeking the return of an investment of $50,000 in Real Estate Investment Trust product 
(REIT) purchased in October 2013 and June 2014. Respondent filed an Answer and a separate 
Request for Expungement. Respondent raised the issue of eligibility and filed a Motion to 
Dismiss. Respondent argues that the Claim is ineligible to be filed in FINRA due to Rule 12206.
FINRA Rule 12206 states that “No claim shall be eligible for submission to arbitration under the 
Code where six years have elapsed from the occurrence or event giving rise to the claim.” The 
question before this Arbitrator is determining the event that triggers the six year period.
The Claim alleges that Respondent sold to Claimants, $50,000 in a REIT product, in two 
separate transactions in 2013 and 2014, that was unsuitable to meet the needs of Claimants, 
who are elderly, have limited education and limited experience in investments. The Claimants’ 
asserted position is that they wanted to protect their $50,000 investment. The Claim further 
alleges that Respondent represented that the principal was protected, and that the REIT would 
return the initial investment of $50,000 after seven years. In addition, the Claim alleges that 
Respondent failed to advise the Claimants that their investment was at risk, misrepresented the 
risk to the principal and failed to advise that the REIT could reduce or fail to pay dividends or 
distributions to the investors. According to the Claim, the relationship was on-going and, in 
September 2018 Respondent sold an annuity to the couple in which the couple transferred their 
interest in a separate annuity to a new one.
In response to the Motion to Dismiss, the Claimants include with their opposition memorandum 
of law, two documents that bear additional information on the Claim. The first is an affidavit 
signed by one of the Claimants that in May 2018, Claimant became concerned that the REIT 
was not a principal protected investment. The affidavit states that his son then emailed the 
Respondent raising serious concerns about the investment. The Claimants assert that there 
were verbal reassurances from Respondent that the principal was protected, but no timeframe 
dates are alleged. The second document is the email from the son dated May 4, 2018, raising 
the issue of unsuitability, and requesting an exit strategy from this investment. The email further 
states the account statements received by his father showed that the value of the REIT 
declining for months. The son further states that the father contacted the company directly and 
was advised that his principal was not protected in this type of investment. The son also 
describes a conversation wherein the Respondent told the father that the REIT could be “bought 
out” and the son then requested whether the Claimants could get out of the investment without 
suffering a significant loss. According to the Claimant’s affidavit, Respondent failed to respond 
to the email.
Based on the Claim, the Answer, the Motion to Dismiss with attachments, the opposition to 
Motion to Dismiss with attachments, the Reply with attachments and the oral arguments of the 
parties at the Prehearing Conference, the Arbitrator finds that the misrepresentation and 
allegations of unsuitability occurred at the time the product was purchased in 2013 and in 2014. 
Although the Claim alleges that the Respondent engaged in a pattern of misrepresentation and 
recommendations of unsuitability products to other clients, the Claim itself does not allege 
misrepresentation and unsuitability beyond the initial recommendation of the REIT for these 
Claimants. The affidavit and email from the son do not cure the Claim’s deficiencies. At best, 
they showed that the Claimants became aware that the principal was not protected, and that the 
product was declining in value months before the May 3, 2018, email. By the Claimant's own 
admission, the Respondent did not reply to the email. It should be noted that Claimant, in his 
affidavit, asserted that in May 2018 that he and his wife had not realized how the product had 
been misrepresented to them but the son’s email and the affidavit itself shows that they were 
questioning Respondent’s alleged representations prior to May 2018. Although there was an 
ongoing relationship with Respondent, the Claim does not allege any facts after the initial 
investment that would lead to a different event that would trigger the eligibility timeline.
Claimants’ attorney raised an argument at the Prehearing Conference that the 2018 
recommendation from Respondent and Claimants’ purchase of an annuity was part of an on-
going investment strategy. However, on the basis of the facts as alleged in this case, the 2018 
annuity purchase and the 2014 and 2013 REIT purchases are too remote to constitute an on-
going investment strategy.
The Motion to Dismiss is granted is granted based upon the above. The Claim was filed over 
nine years after the triggering event or occurrence (the last purchase of the REIT) took place.
Respondent’s Motion to Dismiss pursuant to Rule 12206 of the Code is granted by the Arbitrator 
without prejudice to any right Claimant has to file in court; Claimants are not prohibited from 
pursuing their claims in court pursuant to Rule 12206(b) of the Code. 
On December 9, 2024, Respondent withdrew the request for expungement. On December 12, 
2024, the Arbitrator issued an order pursuant to FINRA Rule 12800(d)(1)(C) denying the request 
for expungement (Occurrence Number 2259974) with prejudice.

hearings, and any post-hearing submissions, the Panel has decided in full and final resolution of 
the issues submitted for determination as follows: 
1. Claimant’s claim for $1.00 in compensatory damages is denied. 
2. The Panel awards the expungement of all references to Occurrence Number 2309573 from 
registration records maintained by the CRD for Claimant E. Matthew Steinberg (CRD 
Number 2430032) with the understanding that, pursuant to Rule 2080, Claimant E. Matthew 
Steinberg must obtain confirmation from a court of competent jurisdiction before the CRD will 
execute the expungement directive. 
Unless specifically waived in writing by FINRA, parties seeking judicial confirmation of an 
arbitration award containing customer dispute expungement relief must name FINRA as an 
additional party and serve FINRA with all appropriate documents. 
Pursuant to Rule 13805 of the Code, the Panel has made the following affirmative finding of 
fact: 
The claim, allegation, or information is false.
The Panel has made the above finding based on the following reasons: 
E. Matthew Steinberg was the Customer’s Financial Advisor. Customer did not name Mr. 
Steinberg as a Respondent in his case against Oppenheimer & Co., Inc., but 
Oppenheimer properly reported the arbitration on Mr. Steinberg’s CRD. There is no other 
customer complaint on Mr. Steinberg’s CRD.
Customer and Oppenheimer reached a settlement prior to the arbitration hearing. Mr. 
Steinberg was not involved in the settlement negotiations or discussions. Claimant was 
told of the total settlement agreement and later was told by Oppenheimer that he was 
expected to contribute 50%. Claimant never saw the actual settlement agreement before 
he agreed to pay Oppenheimer. He had checked with other brokers and found out that it 
was not an unusual request by Oppenheimer. After 30 years with Oppenheimer, he did 
not want to switch brokerage firms.
Customer was a tax attorney, a serial entrepreneur, and an experienced investor. He was 
controlling his account by not only taking all income generated out of his nondiscretionary 
account, but moved into writing checks for withdrawals, borrowing large sums on margin 
against his assets for building a house, and finally taking daily continuous withdrawals to 
pay for his American Express charges. Customer continued to give specific instructions 
of which bonds to be sold to cover his cash withdrawals. Despite repeated requests and 
warnings from Mr. Steinberg about Customer’s continuous withdrawing to pay credit card 
bills and using margin, Customer, knowingly and deliberately, chose to continue to 
withdrawing cash.
The Panel concludes that the Customer’s complaint was both not directed at Mr. 
Steinberg’s action and was false in regard to any action by Mr. Steinberg.

After considering the pleadings, the testimony and evidence presented at the hearing, and any 
post-hearing submissions, the Arbitrator has decided in full and final resolution of the issues 
submitted for determination as follows: 
1. Claimant’s claims are denied in their entirety. 
2.Any and all claims for relief not specifically addressed herein, including any request for 
punitive damages, are denied. 
EXPLANATION OF DECISION
The hearing was a Simplified Arbitration Pursuant to FINRA Rule 12800, in particular Rule 
12800(c)(3)(A).
Gary Braver (the “Claimant”) alleged that his day order (the “Day Order”) to sell 25 shares of Netflix, 
placed on the NASDAQ market exchanges on January 23, 2024, with a limit of price of $496.50, 
should have been cancelled precisely at 4:00 pm on that date. Fidelity Brokerage Services, LLC 
(the “Respondent”) claimed that the Day Order was subject to a NASDAQ procedure known as the 
“Closing Cross,” whereby the Day Order was kept active for milliseconds beyond 4 PM.
In particular, a document produced by NASDAQ (Exhibit C-3) showed a designation of “Cross=N” 
which Claimant alleged meant that the Day Order was not subject to the Closing Cross. However, 
the Claimant did not produce any supporting or corroborating evidence of what that term actually 
meant, nor did any of the Respondent’s witnesses testify under cross examination that they had 
any knowledge of its meaning.
In fact, the Day Order was executed at the limit price of $496.50 at 38 milliseconds after 4:00 pm, 
or 4:00;00:038. The Claimant was paid the proceeds of that transaction. The Claimant alleges that 
he was damaged by virtue of the fact that, had the Day Order been cancelled at 4:00 PM, he would 
have been able to take advantage of the increase in the stock price of Netflix on subsequent 
trading days. The Respondent claimed that the trade was properly executed and that the Claimant 
suffered no damages.
The Claimant also sought punitive damages for the Respondent’s alleged “doctoring” of documents 
to disadvantage him.
The Claimant produced no definitive or substantive evidence that the Respondent’s conduct was 
contrary to the rules of either NASDAQ or FINRA. Accordingly, the Claimant has failed to prove his 
case for any damages resulting from the execution of the Day Order. Further, the Claimant 
produced no evidence of any wrongful conduct on the part of the Respondent and, therefore, could 
not demonstrate entitlement to punitive damages.
Therefore, the Claimant’s claim in this matter is denied in its entirety.

award:
After considering the pleadings, the testimony and evidence presented at the expungement 
hearing, and any post-hearing submissions, the Panel has decided in full and final resolution of 
the issues submitted for determination as follows: 
1. Claimant William Cole Smith’s (CRD Number 5327357) request for expungement of 
Occurrence Number 2253367 from registration records maintained by the CRD is denied 
with prejudice. The Panel’s decision was unanimous. 
The Panel has made the above finding based on the following reasons: 
Key Facts
Claimant is a registered representative and investment advisor. Between August 2010 and 
October 2016, Claimant was registered with Lincoln Financial Advisors Corporation 
(“Lincoln”) now known as Respondent OSAIC Wealth, Inc. as an independent contractor.
In 2015, Claimant recommended that the Customer, a government contractor, purchase a
$100,000.00 investment in Atlas Growth Partners, L.P. (“Atlas”), an oil and gas investment 
private fund.
Claimant testified that Respondent had approved Atlas for investment by customers. 
Claimant believed Atlas was a suitable investment for the Customer because the company’s 
tax advisor had recommended tax-advantaged investments to offset the Customer’s growing 
income.
Atlas did not perform as expected and declared bankruptcy in 2021. On December 28,
2022, the Customer, along with other Atlas investors, filed an arbitration claim against 
Respondent seeking compensatory damages. The claim does not name Claimant as a party 
but alleges that he “failed in his due diligence by not giving them [the Customer] the proper 
information about their investment.”
This allegation was reported on Claimant’s BrokerCheck® report as Occurrence Number
2253367. The report says that Claimant “recommended an unsuitable Oil & Gas
investment.” The alleged damages are $100,000.00 (the amount invested). The outcome is a
settlement for $79,721.09 to which Claimant contributed nothing.
Claimant vehemently denies any responsibility for the loss in his BrokerCheck® report and
filed this claim to have this occurrence expunged. According to Claimant, the Customer did 
not blame him for recommending Atlas and remains a client to this day.
The Initial Prehearing Conference Order in this matter states in paragraph 38: “Claimant
does not have settlement documents in hand and will provide whatever is furnished in 
discovery. Lincoln is hereby ordered to produce the settlement agreements.”
Governing Law
FINRA Rule 13805 governs expungement requests that are separate from customer 
litigation. Subsection (b)(8) tasks the Panel with reviewing settlement documents to 
determine whether the broker seeking expungement paid to settle the claim, and whether the 
customer agreed not to oppose expungement in exchange for this payment. 
Subsection (b)(9) allows a panel to expunge a customer dispute only if it unanimously finds 
that:
a. the claim, allegation or information is factually impossible or clearly erroneous;
b. the registered person was not involved in the alleged investment-related sales practice 
violation, forgery, theft, misappropriation or conversion of funds; or
c. the claim, allegation or information is false.
Analysis and Conclusion
Settlement Agreement
Respondent did not comply with the Panel’s order to produce the settlement agreement. This 
is not Claimant’s fault. Claimant testified that he had no role in negotiating the settlement and 
contributed nothing to the payout. Claimant’s testimony is credible because he was not a 
party to the claim, and his BrokerCheck® report shows no contribution from personal funds.
Grounds for Expungement
Claimant seeks expungement under all three permitted grounds. While the record contains
no proof of wrongdoing by Claimant, his uncorroborated testimony is not sufficient to meet 
the high bar for expungement. Respondent paid just under 80% of the amount sought to 
settle an arbitration claim which casts blame on Claimant. If, as Claimant asserts, the 
Customer’s principals were not aware of and did not support the assertion in their arbitration 
claim that Claimant was at fault, he should have had at least one of the principals testify on 
his behalf or sign a letter supporting his request for expungement. The record is insufficient 
to show that the challenged customer complaint is clearly erroneous or false, or that Claimant 
had nothing to do with the transaction.
